tells: 'the prayer Imam ʿAli (as) taught to Kumayl ibn Ziyad ... when many of us hear it' — concrete setting, shared 'us', each paragraph picks up the last ('A request for God's love begins to answer the question Chapter Two ended on'); plain declaratives, no flourish

'Sheikh Bahmanpour uses hunger to describe a kind of knowing that differs from the kind gained by study' / 'Most of what we know of God is of the kind gained by study' — the second paragraph opens by repeating the last phrase of the first, Author A's habit; plain 'we', no scolding, the image is explained at once

'The prayers go on to ask for three things: ... Let's take them in turn.' — numbered plan with 'Let's', then 'The first is sight' picking it up; the Sheikh's point is paraphrased and the quotation's purpose stated ('The prayer asks God to give that inner eye light to see by')

'It is rooted in the Qur'an and the Imams. It is walked by a tested and ordered method. And it ends not in withdrawal from the world but in return' — anaphoric triplet and a sentence opening on 'And'; Author A would write one linked sentence and never opens with 'And'
'some of the words you'll meet' — contraction and 'you'; Author A addresses the reader as 'we' and 'most of us', never 'you'll'
'a guide to beginning the journey that strives for brevity and clarity' — a book praising its own virtues in abstract nouns; Author A states what a chapter does, not what it strives for
'Additional call-out sections are spread throughout with helpful context and short side notes' — 'helpful' is a puff word; Author A would write 'Boxes give context' or leave it out
'None of it is exotic.' — a one-line punch sentence; Author A would fold it into the list sentence ('The signs are all around us: in marriage, ...')
'reflecting, knowing, listening, reasoning' and 'sleep, earning a living, a storm, rain' — asyndeton; Author A writes lists with 'and' before the last item ('reflect, know, listen and reason')
'The Qur'an is not asking for a new set of duties. It is asking whether we perceive' — the 'not X. It is Y' antithesis pair; Author A states the point once without the rhetorical setup

'to see, in the marriage and the sleep and the rain, the One whose signs they are' — 'and'-chain plus a lyrical capitalised 'the One' as a closing cadence; Author A ends paragraphs on a plain statement ('Most of us see only the lamp')
'has called for some editorial adaptation' — abstract, administrative phrasing; Author A would say what changed ('has meant reordering and cutting')

'To suit a wider readership, the book also adds context and explanation to support its main arguments' — vague abstract nouns ('context and explanation', 'main arguments'); Author A names the thing added
'It draws on a wider literature as well' — 'wider' twice in two sentences and 'literature' as an abstract mass; Author A writes 'other books' or names them first

'"without this", the Sheikh says, "there is no maʿrifah". Purification, in his account, is polishing the soul so that it starts working. It is the repair of the rusted faculty that Chapter One described.' — quotation spoken to immediately, cross-reference made in a plain clause, next paragraph opens on 'Having done this'

'Sheikh Bahmanpour sets two words against each other. The knowledge learned at a university or a seminary comes through fikr, thought: we think, put things together, analyse and find out.' — term, gloss, concrete list ending in 'and'; the closing 'Purification is the traveller's part; the light is Allah's to give' matches 'God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them'

'It shares its root with maʿrifah, knowledge and an ʿarif is, in Sheikh Bahmanpour's words, "someone who knows"' — short quotation embedded and immediately used; 'the Islam we already know' keeps the shared 'we'; no rhetorical build-up

'Whatever stands between the heart and the light stands on our side' and 'Chapter One reached the same conclusion by another road, when it placed the fault in the receiver' — the reference's own 'the fault is on our side' logic, Khomeini quotation introduced and then explained, paragraph linked back to the previous one

'Reason has a limit and Sheikh Bahmanpour says where it lies' — the reference's exact construction ('The Qur'an says where it lies'); concrete examples ('brown or square or useful'), then 'If this is true of the things around us, it is true far more of God' as a plain step
'remain an ongoing conversation among our ʿulamaʾ' — 'ongoing conversation' is a stock abstract phrase; Author A would write 'the scholars still differ on'
'this book presents each view with neutrality' — abstract noun where Author A would use a plain adverb or verb ('sets out each view fairly')

'Three guiding principles frame the discussions in the chapters that follow' — academic framing diction ('guiding principles', 'frame the discussions'); Author A would write 'Three things hold throughout the book'
'How this position differs from that of the Sufi orders is explored in Chapter Nine' — passive 'is explored'; Author A writes 'Chapter Nine shows how'

'"O my Master, (please) expel love for the world out of my heart," it asks ... What the prayer asks to lose is the heart's love for the world, not the world itself' — quotation then plain explanation of what it does and does not mean; opens on 'therefore' picking up the last paragraph; 'the friends of God, who keep their families and their place in society' echoes the reference

'Let's start with the order in which the prayers ask' — the reference's 'Let's start with two claims'; 'Sheikh Bahmanpour asks whether it is good to be cut off completely from everything else. In the heart, he answers, it is.' — the Sheikh's question answered at once, no rhetorical hang

'For some of us, the Sheikh says, calling on God can feel like calling into the sky to someone far away' — homely image attributed and plainly explained; Mutahhari quotation introduced, given, then its purpose stated ('He cites them to show that')
'asks why a believer should bother' — colloquial 'bother'; Author A would write 'why a believer should pursue it'
'with a compatible view of similarities to Sufism' — tangled abstract phrase; Author A would write 'and how it stands to Sufism'

'describes the landscape a traveller passes through on the journey towards ʿirfan: the self' — metaphor stretched over a clause before the colon reveals the subject; Author A names the thing first ('the self, which the traveller passes through')
'as an endeavour for the ordinary believer' — abstract noun 'endeavour' used oddly; Author A would write 'for ordinary believers to say'
'in our munajats and on auspicious occasions' — stock pious phrase; Author A names the occasion ('at weddings', 'on Thursday evening')
'does not feature in our day-to-day routine' and 'are the dominant undertaking' — managerial diction; Author A would write 'is not part of most days' and 'are most of what we do'

'Hunger, the example this chapter opened with, is another and so is pain' — picks up the chapter's own earlier image; 'The hunger may even be false, the Sheikh notes, yet the feeling is real and drives us' — attribution mid-sentence, concrete case, balanced semicolon close ('the cause is not the feeling')
